about: I'm a developer in Cairo. I build AI-agent pipelines end to end — the retrieval, the evaluation, the command line — and I run the Linux underneath them: immutable Fedora images built from a Containerfile, Nix flakes, systemd units, containers.

Most of what I ship starts as a tool I needed and ends as a repository someone else can install. I care about tools that tell the truth about what they did: docpipe refuses to build an index it can't trace back to real files on disk; langpipe reports what you actually retained instead of a streak count.

That instinct comes from having to keep the systems alive as well as write them. Both my desktop and my laptop boot images I build and sign myself, and the same repository carries the drivers, the desktop and the hardware quirks. I'm finishing a B.A. in Business Administration at Ain Shams University, and I taught programming for two years before I started taking contract work.
current: Hardening docpipe and langpipe, and reading for my final year at Ain Shams.

experience.summary: Rebuilt the project's REST API layer and shipped it to a Debian production stack.
bullets: Rebuilt the project's REST API layer, replacing per-request full-table work with an indexed query path — a measured ~160× improvement in response time.
Shipped and monitored the change on a Debian production stack: systemd services, a packaged Python environment, and log review on deploy.
Wrote the migration notes and tests so the change could be reviewed and rolled forward by maintainers.

experience.summary: Built and maintained three production Discord bots for paying communities.
bullets: Built and maintained three production Discord bots for paying communities: QuickFlips (eBay deal search), ProBotX (moderation, games, utilities) and Infinity-Team (team and payout management).
Owned the whole loop — requirements, hosting, scheduled jobs, support — for users who noticed every minute of downtime.

experience.summary: Taught beginner programming sessions to small groups.
bullets: Taught beginner programming sessions to small groups, wrote the lesson material and ran the lab exercises.
Learned to explain a stack trace without jargon — still the most useful habit I have when writing documentation.

projects.name: docpipe
projects.oneLiner: Hashes a folder of text, markdown and PDFs, then builds a SQLite index you can query by term, vector or hybrid — and refuses to build if any row can't be traced back to a real file.

projects.name: langpipe
projects.oneLiner: Turns a word list and grammar points into a working study plan: generated practice cards, SM-2 spaced repetition, honest retention stats and an idempotent Anki sync.

projects.name: book-man
projects.oneLiner: A dyslexia-friendly study companion that converts a PDF or EPUB textbook into a flat Obsidian wiki the agent queries — and keeps filing answers back into it.

projects.name: agent-skills
projects.oneLiner: Twelve first-hand skills for coding agents — Fedora Atomic ops, PDF tooling, browser automation, editor integration — each loaded only when a task matches it.

projects.name: mina-fedora-atomic
projects.oneLiner: A personal Fedora Atomic image built from a twelve-stage Containerfile: OS, drivers, desktop and hardware quirks all in the repo — two hardware profiles from one source.

projects.name: nix-mina
projects.oneLiner: A personal Nix flake for my own machines: MangoWC, Dank Material Shell and Home Manager modules in a single reproducible tree.

projects.name: QuickFlips
projects.oneLiner: A Discord bot that watches eBay listings for underpriced items and pushes the good ones to subscribers, with per-user search options and filters.

projects.name: ProBotX
projects.oneLiner: An all-in-one Discord bot for server management — moderation, games and utilities — run in live communities with a small web dashboard.

projects.name: Infinity-Team
projects.oneLiner: A Discord bot for managing Axie Infinity teams: scholarships, team rosters and payout tracking in one place instead of a spreadsheet.

education.note: Cloud fundamentals, billing and the shared-responsibility model — enough to talk to the infrastructure rather than guess at it.
Learned the way I still learn it: build the thing, break the thing, write down what broke.
